full_texts.title: KISR develops polymer fibers to improve reinforced concrete - Kuwait Times
full_texts.text:
KUWAIT: The Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research (KISR) announced Sunday the completion of a research project to develop synthetic polymer fibers made from polypropylene and polyethylene to improve reinforced concrete properties and enhance its resistance to impacts and cracking.
In a press statement, KISR said the project was carried out by its Petroleum Research Center, headed by Petrochemicals and Materials Technology Program Director Dr Salah Al-Enezi, in cooperation with Equate Petrochemical Company and with support from the Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences (KFAS).
The project resulted in the development of polymer fibers made from polypropylene and linear low-density polyethylene (PP/LLDPE) blends that can be manufactured and used in concrete.
Tests showed that fiber-reinforced concrete had improved impact resistance, greater toughness and a better ability to withstand loads after cracking, while the effect on compressive strength was limited. KISR said the project aims to maximize the added value of locally available polymers by converting them into specialized engineering products that support the construction sector and national industry.
The project also identified potential applications for the developed fibers in industrial flooring, pavements and precast concrete elements. Its findings were submitted for publication in the international peer-reviewed Journal of Building Engineering. KISR said the project is part of its efforts to develop innovative scientific and technological solutions, make better use of local materials and strengthen cooperation between the research and industrial sectors in support of sustainable development in Kuwait. — KUNA

According to informed sources, the ongoing construction reflects a shift in the government’s approach from planning to implementation. By the end of this decade, Kuwait is expected to see a significant increase in foreign investment, which will play a crucial role in diversifying national income sources, creating employment opportunities in non-oil sectors and strengthening the local economy’s integration into global supply chains. The sources revealed that KDIPA is moving ahead with efforts to reshape Kuwait’s economic landscape.
They explained that KDIPA, through a comprehensive portfolio of investment-ready opportunities in strategic locations, aims to strengthen Kuwait’s position as a competitive regional investment hub, attract international capital and encourage the localization of advanced technologies and innovation. The initiative involves developing land allocated to KDIPA, covering an estimated total area of 19 square kilometers. This extensive area is expected to be transformed into attractive destinations for foreign direct investment (FDI), offering fully developed land and facilities suitable for industrial, technological and logistics businesses. This will enable foreign investors to enter the Kuwaiti market while benefiting from competitive investment advantages.
Regarding the project’s development and social impact, the sources noted that its expected benefits extend well beyond financial returns. At its core, the project aims to bring modern technologies and advanced technical expertise into Kuwait while creating high-quality, sustainable job opportunities for young Kuwaitis in innovative sectors. It will also provide opportunities to develop local skills and train national professionals to meet the highest international standards. The sources stressed that diversifying Kuwait’s national income is no longer simply an option but an essential requirement for ensuring the country’s long-term economic future.
They affirmed that linking these economic zones to the “value-added” concept is primarily aimed at attracting advanced manufacturing, technology and logistics industries. These sectors would help reduce reliance on oil as the main driver of economic activity while capitalizing on Kuwait’s strategic geographical location to secure a greater share of regional and international supply chain

full_texts.title: Kuwait moves to turn seven historic landmarks into investment, hotel destinations - Times Kuwait
full_texts.text:
Kuwait is preparing to turn seven historic buildings and sites into commercial, hotel and cultural destinations as part of a broader plan to unlock the economic value of heritage assets, attract private investment and revitalize the capital’s city center.
The initiative marks a shift in the way the government views historic properties, moving beyond the traditional approach of spending on restoration and maintenance towards finding sustainable uses that can generate revenue, support businesses and preserve Kuwait’s architectural and cultural identity.
The initial development plan covers the Mishref Palace, the old Chest Hospital and Al-Mubarakiya School. Four additional sites that are being considered are Fahad Al-Salem Palace, the Awqaf Complex, the Palace of Justice and Safafir Market, also known as the Coppersmiths’ Market.
The authorities are also examining a proposal to revive the Qibla Cultural District by connecting unused spaces and heritage locations into an integrated cultural and commercial destination.
The Public-Private Partnership Projects Authority has already presented a project to prepare and develop educational infrastructure for the creative economy under the National Council for Culture, Arts and Letters’ strategic roadmap.
The first phase focuses on the three initial locations, while the National Council, in cooperation with the Public Authority for Industry and the Ministry of Finance, is studying how the other sites could be incorporated into the development program.
The proposals offer different investment possibilities based on the character and location of each property. Fahad Al-Salem Palace, opposite the Amiri Hospital, is being considered for conversion into a boutique hotel or entertainment destination, subject to site assessments and feasibility studies.
The Palace of Justice could be repurposed as a heritage hotel hosting cultural events and activities, while the Al-Mubarakiya School could be linked more closely to the traditional market and used for design, architecture and urban planning activities.
Safafir Market is expected to play a crucial role in developing the creative economy by moving beyond its traditional retail function and becoming a center for crafts, creative manufacturing and related productive activities.
The National Council has submitted a proposal to the Public Authority for Industry to use the market as part of efforts to revive central Kuwait City, attract private-sector investment and create opportunities for local craftspeople and creative businesses.
The proposed revival of the Qibla Cultural District would connect Qibla School, the National Museum and the National Library with the Al-Mubarakiya School and the inner market. The aim is to create a more connected urban destination capable of attracting cultural, commercial and tourism activities.
The Awqaf Complex is also under review, with authorities examining a more integrated economic and cultural use for the property. The assessment takes into account its high capital cost and the challenges of achieving strong occupancy rates in central Kuwait City.
The plan extends beyond heritage buildings to the country’s network of 56 public libraries. Authorities are considering ways to expand their role as spaces for learning, research, design and innovation, while hosting exhibitions, workshops, professional programs and cultural events in cooperation with private-sector companies and cultural institutions.
The proposals also seek to diversify funding, improve operational efficiency and measure the libraries’ wider social, educational and economic contribution. For investors, the proposed program could open opportunities in hospitality, cultural tourism, creative manufacturing, design, event management and the operation of heritage properties. It could also create business opportunities for small enterprises, designers, artisans and other professionals linked to the creative industries.
However, the projects remain at the conceptual, feasibility-study and private-sector consultation stages. No investment requirements, projected financial returns or implementation schedules have yet been announced.
Their commercial viability will depend on the development models adopted, operating costs, investor participation and the ability to attract sustained demand without compromising the heritage value of the properties.
Legislative framework
Alongside the property development plan, government agencies are working with the Ministry of Finance, the Civil Service Bureau and the Fatwa and Legislation Department to prepare a draft decree-law governing creative industries.
The proposed legislation is intended to provide a more flexible framework for cultural and creative businesses, allowing the National Council to expand partnerships with private investors and attract creative talent.
It is also expected to establish clearer arrangements for financing, project operation and risk management, helping ensure the long-term sustainability of investments while protecting the cultural and historical value of the assets.
The initiative comes as Kuwait seeks to diversify its sources of income and strengthen its knowledge-based economy. By putting underused public properties to productive use, the government aims to combine heritage preservation with commercial activity, support local businesses and position Kuwait as a regional destination for design and creative industries.
